sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Early Clues to Inflammatory Myopathy
sections.description: Walk through the patient’s timeline from semaglutide exposure to progressive neuromuscular symptoms, highlighting bedside findings and initial labs that raised concern for an autoimmune myopathy rather than toxic rhabdomyolysis.
subtopics: Index exposure: single 0.25 mg SC semaglutide dose; immediate severe GI intolerance, hypovolemia, AKI, modest CK elevation (~300s U/L)
Evolution over 4 months: progressive proximal limb weakness, dysphagia, dysphonia; inability to sit/stand without assistance; absence of rash or myalgias
Examination pattern: symmetric proximal>distal weakness without skin or synovial findings
Laboratory signal: rising CK to ~4000 U/L; AST/ALT elevation in context of known NAFLD; inflammatory markers mildly elevated; normal TSH
Imaging and ancillary testing highlights: thigh MRI with symmetric muscle edema; cardiac biomarkers and imaging suggesting transient myocardial edema without scar
Red flags favoring inflammatory myopathy: subacute progression, bulbar involvement, MRI myoedema, CK trajectory, and lack of rapid CK resolution expected with toxic rhabdomyolysis

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning: From Broad Differential to Confirmed IMNM
sections.description: Outline a structured approach to proximal weakness with CK elevation, and demonstrate how this case was narrowed to immune-mediated necrotising myopathy using targeted serologies, imaging, and biopsy.
subtopics: Differential diagnosis: drug/toxic rhabdomyolysis; statin-associated IMNM; idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IMNM, dermatomyositis, polymyositis), inclusion body myositis, endocrine/metabolic myopathies, motor neuron disease, neuromuscular junction disorders

Key discriminators: CK time course (delayed peak vs immediate spike), presence/absence of myalgia and pigmenturia, skin findings, distribution of weakness, EMG/MRI features (MRI myoedema supporting active myositis)
Autoantibody testing: myositis-specific and -associated panels (HMGCR, SRP, antisynthetase, Mi-2, MDA5, TIF1-γ, NXP2, cN1A); interpretation of negative panel in seronegative IMNM
Transaminase source analysis: distinguishing hepatic vs muscle origin; role of prior and repeat liver biopsy confirming progression of NAFLD independent of CK trend
Cardiac assessment in inflammatory myopathy: interpreting modest hs-troponin/BNP elevations; echocardiography and cardiac MRI to exclude overt myocarditis
Indications for muscle biopsy and expected findings supporting IMNM
Synthesis in this case: seronegative IMNM favored by clinical course, MRI edema, and definitive biopsy despite negative autoantibodies

sections.section_title: IMNM Essentials: Pathophysiology, Serologies, and Histopathology
sections.description: Provide focused background on IMNM necessary to interpret this case, emphasizing immune mechanisms, serologic phenotypes, and biopsy hallmarks that distinguish IMNM from other myopathies.
subtopics: Definition and epidemiology of IMNM; aggressive proximal weakness with high CK and paucity of lymphocytes on histology
Autoantibody subsets: anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP phenotypes vs seronegative IMNM (~one-third of cases)
Pathogenesis: complement-mediated myofiber necrosis; macrophage-predominant myophagocytosis; limited T-cell infiltrates

Biopsy features in this patient: scattered necrotic/regenerating fibers; CD68+ macrophages; acid phosphatase activity; membrane attack complex (MAC) deposition on necrotic and non-necrotic fibers; rare CD3+ cells and perivascular inflammation
Differentiation from polymyositis/dermatomyositis (endomysial T cells or perifascicular atrophy) and from toxic rhabdomyolysis (necrosis without immune signatures)
Known triggers: statins (HMGCR autoimmunity), other drugs/infections; implications for recognizing new potential triggers

sections.section_title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Muscle Injury: Association, Mechanisms, and Causality
sections.description: Examine how semaglutide could relate to IMNM, contrast with known GLP-1RA-associated rhabdomyolysis, and apply causality frameworks to this case while outlining plausible mechanisms and clinical implications.
subtopics: Semaglutide and GLP-1RA pharmacology and indications (obesity, type 2 diabetes); common adverse effects (GI) and lean mass loss
Published neuromuscular events: rhabdomyolysis with tirzepatide demonstrating acute CK spike and rapid resolution after withdrawal
Why this case fits IMNM rather than rhabdomyolysis: delayed CK rise over months, need for immunosuppression, biopsy with immune signatures, sustained remission after brief therapy and drug cessation

Causality assessment: applying WHO-Uppsala Monitoring Centre (UMC) criteria—temporal relationship, exclusion of alternatives, response to withdrawal—supporting a ‘probable’ association; rationale against rechallenge

Hypothesized mechanisms: drug-triggered immune dysregulation, molecular mimicry/unmasking of muscle antigens, metabolic stress priming immunity; role of early dehydration/AKI as a confounder but insufficient explanation
Clinical guidance: avoid GLP-1RA rechallenge after suspected IMNM; patient counseling; encourage pharmacovigilance reporting; research needs to identify predisposing factors

sections.description: Translate the diagnostic conclusion into a management plan tailored to IMNM with suspected drug trigger, including immunotherapy choices, monitoring, complication mitigation, and long-term outcomes.
subtopics: Initial therapy: pulse IV methylprednisolone followed by high-dose oral prednisone (≈1 mg/kg/day)
Role of IVIG (2 g/kg over 2–5 days) for severe features (bulbar involvement, marked weakness) or when rapid response is needed
When to add/stagger steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, mycophenolate, rituximab) in idiopathic/refractory IMNM vs drug-induced cases often improving with brief course
Monitoring: serial CK/AST-ALT, quantitative strength testing, swallow and respiratory assessments, MRI utility, and cardiac surveillance when biomarkers/imaging are abnormal
Tapering strategy: criteria for accelerated taper in responders; relapse vigilance after discontinuation
Preventing and managing complications: infection risk on high-dose steroids/IVIG (e.g., pseudomonal UTI sepsis), vaccination, osteoporosis prophylaxis, VTE considerations
Rehabilitation and recovery milestones; nutritional strategies to preserve/restore muscle mass
Long-term plan: avoidance of GLP-1RAs, shared decision-making on weight management alternatives, follow-up intervals, and triggers for re-evaluation
Key takeaways: recognize seronegative IMNM; differentiate from toxic rhabdomyolysis by time course/biopsy; consider new drugs as potential triggers; act early with immunotherapy when IMNM suspected
